title: Charter Stock Sinks As Internet Subscriber Losses Worsen; Could A Comcast Merger Be The Next Move?
full_text: Skip to main content By Dade Hayes Dade Hayes Business Editor @dadehayes More Stories By Dade Fox Corp. Closes $22 Billion Acquisition Of Roku Online Media Pioneer Salon To Shutter: “Our Publishing Model Is No Longer Sustainable” Netflix Woos Mattel Veteran Roberto Stanichi To Lead Consumer Products and Experiences View All November 6, 2026 8:40am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Charter Communications Photo Illustration by Igor Golovniov/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Charter Communications shares fell 5% in early trading Friday after the pay-TV, broadband and wireless provider reported wider internet subscriber losses in the third quarter. During the quarter, in August, Charter closed its $34.5 billion acquisition of rival Cox Communications, expanding its footprint to 45 states. Quarterly results, reported on a pro forma basis to account for the merger, showed continued erosion of internet and pay-TV customers. Wireless remains a comparative bright spot, with 1.8 million sign-ups over the past year giving the company 13.5 million wireless customers as of September 30. Related Stories News Online Media Pioneer Salon To Shutter: "Our Publishing Model Is No Longer Sustainable" News Lionsgate Quarterly Revenue Pops With Growth Across Film & TV Studios, Library The company shed 233,000 internet customers – 156,000 at legacy Charter and 77,000 at legacy Cox – in the quarter. The subscriber total sat at 34.3 million as of the end of the quarter. Wireless and satellite internet providers, including Elon Musk’s Starlink, have put pressure on major broadband players like Charter and fueled speculation about a potential Charter-Comcast tie-up. Comcast is about to split off NBCUniversal from its connectivity business, which faces similar headwinds. Watch on Deadline Along with the quarterly results, CEO Chris Winfrey unveiled plans to cut $2 billion in costs and reaffirmed a projection for $1 billion in merger-related synergies. Investors seemed underwhelmed, with Friday’s downturn in the stock price extending a 43% drop in 2026 to date. Cord-cutting continues to eat away at pay-TV levels, even though Charter’s Spectrum systems have integrated streaming services aggressively enough to stem the downturn more than many operators. Total video customers fell by 77,000 in the quarter, compared with a decline of 121,000 a year ago. The total subscriber base was 13.8 million at the end of the quarter. Total company revenue rose 9% over the year-earlier period, reaching $14.9 billion. Gregory Williams, an analyst for TD Cowen, anticipated the Friday trade in a client note earlier this week. “Investors may not get constructive until they see a resting place on broadband subscriber losses,” he wrote. “The next catalyst could be a Comcast/Charter tie-up, which may need to occur sooner rather than later given the midterm election results as a broader regulatory signal.” ‘Stranger Things’ Live-Action Prequel Gets Greenlight At Netflix Kitsch, Daddario, Walken Set For True-Crime Thriller ‘The Long Island Bank Robber’ Fox Closes $22B Takeover Of Roku, Creating Massive New Streaming Player Senator’s Letters Preview Dems’ Plans To Probe FCC, Big Tech & Maybe Mergers Read More About: Comments

title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Sparks Frenzy in Europe as  Screenings Sell Out and Anticipation Soars: ‘People Are Just Desperate to See It’
full_text: × Nov 6, 2026 8:37am PT ‘You Can See Everything’ Sparks Frenzy in Europe as Screenings Sell Out and Anticipation Soars: ‘People Are Just Desperate to See It’ By Elsa Keslassy , Alex Ritman Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy Everett Collection “ You Can See Everything ,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim ’s smash-hit documentary about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, has yet to open in major international territories. But the crescendoing anticipation for a nearly three-hour film that came out of nowhere suggests that it could also rock numerous other box offices in the coming weeks. In the U.K., where A24 is self-releasing the film, tickets began selling out a month before its opening on Nov. 20, prompting chains such as Picturehouse and Cineworld to add extra screenings. It’s a similar story in France, where distributor Metropolitan Filmexport has seen advance screenings sell out far ahead of its opening there on Dec. 30. Related Stories Pamela Abdy Delivers Fiery Speech After Warner Bros. Exit: ‘It Is Getting Harder, Not Easier, to Be a Woman in the Business’ “I’ve released hundreds of films and I’ve not known anything like it in terms of buzz — people are just desperate to see it,” says a distribution exec in the U.K. “I think it’s going to explode on Nov. 20. It’s going to be one of, if not the biggest documentary of all time, just based on pre-bookings.” Excluding concert films, 2004’s “Fahrenheit 9/11” is still the most successful documentary in the U.K. (it’s currently the most successful globally), with a box office of £6.55 million ($8.8 million), which, adjusted for inflation, is around $16.6 million today. It’s a figure many expect “You Can See Everything” to surpass. A24 adopted a staggered release strategy in the U.S., more than tripling the amount of screens in its second weekend. But Variety hears that, to cope with the pent-up demand, it’ll likely bolt out of the British cinematic gates wide, going straight into around 500 cinemas. In France, Victor Hadida, president of Metropolitan Filmexport, tells Variety that the company organized a nationwide series of sneak previews on Dec. 1 across roughly 100 theaters. Tickets sold out within hours. “It’s crazy because we put tickets on sale on Saturday at 9 a.m., and some theaters were already sold out by noon,” says Hadida, whose slate also includes “The Debut.” “The demand is enormous and it hasn’t stopped. You can see it on social media, and you can see people going to theaters asking about the film.” Unlike the U.K., Metropolitan Filmexport — which bought “You Can See Everything” from A24 at Toronto, shortly after it’s surprise Telluride premiere— will be following a similar progressive rollout to the U.S., opening in approximately 150 to 200 theaters before expanding based on demand. Hadida says the nearly three-hour running time was a key factor in scheduling the release during the Christmas holidays, when moviegoers have more time to spare. Metropolitan is betting that the Dec. 1 previews will help build word of mouth — something that has been absolutely crucial in the film’s success so far — ahead of the official opening. But by the time it comes out in France on Dec. 30, much of the rest of the world will already have had a chance to see it. After acquiring large swathes of Europe, Asia, the Middle East and South America for the film before the opening U.S. weekend, Sony has now revealed its release strategy for all of its 29 territories, with opening dates running from Nov. 19 through Dec. 9. Thanks to cultural and language crossovers, not to mention a strong eye for documentary films, especially theatrically, there are high expectations for Scandinavia. Sony has the entire region, and opens across Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden in the space of 48 hours from Nov. 19. There are similar hopes for another major market, Germany (Dec. 3). Highlighting anticipation there, a recent CNN article told the story of a German fan who crossed the border to get to a preview screening in Poland (where it opens Nov. 6). But with other territories such as India, Mexico, South Korea and Brazil on the rollout list and a film that continues to defy the norms or standard expectations, nothing should be ruled out. As one exec notes: “You can’t sell any market short when something becomes cultural like this.” In terms of actual promotional launch plans for “You Can See Everything,” talks are underway to fly Fielder and Oppenheim over to some of the more major premieres. However, as one publicity insider notes, since the film continues to enjoy a wildly unpredictable journey on home soil, plans are likely “very TBC.” With the U.K. likely the biggest overseas market, London would seem a highly probable destination for the pair (Oppenheim was in town in October for the London Film Festival screening of “Primetime”). They’re both due to attend two BAFTA screenings in the capital next week, so assumingly will be stay in town for the premiere, although exact details of that are yet to be revealed. Hadida adds that Metropolitan is hoping to bring them to Paris in December as well. But given the mystery around the film — not to mention some major spoilers to protect — there’s a limit to what anyone would want the filmmakers to actually talk about. Variety hears that the standard premiere media line would likely be scrapped, while any Q&As would likely be held just for awards voters (Fielder and Oppenheim will be taking part in Q&As at the BAFTA screenings in London) “It’s so different to a lot of other PR plans and strategy, because you just don’t want to say anything,” says the publicity insider. “That’s why it’s all so minimal — you just want the film to speak for itself.” Hadida in France also acknowledges that preserving the mystery — which has been a major element of A24’s marketing strategy — is key. “Part of their approach is also not to reveal too much about the film, because what’s important about this experience is that you discover what the film is about at the same time as the filmmakers,” he says. However, among the more eye-opening reveals in “You Can See Everything,” one that saw the film land an unexpected R-rating for “graphic nudity,” won’t be available to everyone. Due to censorship laws in Middle East, Variety hears that the scene in question — not critical but the source of much chatter — will have to be cut for it to be released. ‘One Minute to Midnight’ Review: A Stellar Cast Deliver Interesting but Overly Preachy Disquisitions on the Changing Nature of Male-Female Relations Loading comments...

title: Meet the British Foodie Demystifying the Michelin Guide’s Secrets
full_text: × Skip to main content By Mikey O'Connell Plus Icon Mikey O'Connell Senior Entertainment Editor View All November 6, 2026 8:28am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jesse Burgess in 'Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars.' Apple TV Jesse Burgess is a chef whisperer. If you’re interested in food and have a penchant for scrolling, you may already know this from one of his many vertical clips. The 35-year-old English foodie, host and co-founder of media platform TopJaw, forged a reputation for charming London’s culinary luminaries into opening up not just about their work but the restaurants, bars and Sunday roasts that they adore. And, just as informative, the spots that they think are overrated. Interviewing chef after chef after chef for going on 10 years, Burgess has honed another rather novel skill. He can talk about fine dining without a ring of pretension. “This guy properly reads the fucking room,” says Gordon Ramsay , several times a TopJaw guest. “Jesse understands what he does and doesn’t know. He talks from a viewer’s perspective and lets you in on the secret, what’s going on … where a critic would have the tendency to slide toward being an asshole.” Related Stories TV Apple TV Renews 'Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars' for Season 3 TV Toni Collette to Lead Apple TV Dramedy 'Lenni' An asshole was the last thing Apple TV needed when casting its ambitious culinary series, Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars . The word Michelin already evokes thoughts of white tablecloths, comical price tags, foams, fermentations and microgreens applied via tweezers. (And, you know, the whole tire manufacturing part of the business.) To preemptively deflate perceived elitism, many associated with the project say there was ultimately only one choice to be its face. Gordon Ramsay and Jesse Burgess Photo by Dave Benett/Getty Images for Studio Ramsay “I’d heard about the show, because they had already filmed quite a bit of it without a host, flying to chefs all around the world,” says Burgess, over lunch this past summer in East Hollywood. “I didn’t think I had a hope in hell of getting the job.” The series was being produced by Studio Ramsay Global, so it was Ramsay who suggested Burgess fly out to do a screen test during the first season’s Sweden shoot. “We had a long list of A-listers lining up to present the show, and Apple wanted some of their own talent, but Jesse, from my side, was the running favorite from day one,” says Ramsay. “What makes him special is his vulnerability in these situations” It’s a unique situation in which Burgess found himself. Ostensibly another cooking competition, Knife Edge , which concludes its second season on Nov. 6, follows chefs from around the world as they strive to earn, maintain or up their count of stars in the storied Michelin guide. They punch walls. They weep. They hemorrhage money. They make very appetizing meals. But in lieu of having Burgess exhaustively interview them, he’s almost the translator of their work — narrating the trials of operating a restaurant and describing meals as he eats them with the relatable manner of a thoughtful guy at the pub who just really wants to tell you about his burger. Most episodes include one of Michelin’s many international galas where the stars are announced and presented. Maintaining a distance from the hopeful chefs like he’s Jane Goodall, Burgess takes it all in from the backs of different ballrooms as careers are made and hearts are broken. His empathy and everyman quality make him suitable for this job, but he doesn’t claim to have ever had ambitions for a traditional career in entertainment. Burgess just likes travel and eat and talk about both. Chatting over our respective plates of Somali chicken and grilled fish at East Hollywood Pan-African bistro Foods From Afar (his selection), Burgess traces his curiosity back to his mother’s career as cabin crew on Britannia Airways and then private jets. View this post on Instagram “To me, her life was just so exciting,” he says, recalling how he’d wait for her return and edible souvenirs. “I had Beluga caviar because she’d flown to Russia, Danish pastries from Copenhagen, Stollen from Cologne. She hates me telling these stories because she reckons she wasn’t allowed to take the food out of the country. She thinks that someone’s going to come and arrest her or something.” In 2015, Burgess made eating his business. He partnered with his friend Will Warr and founded TopJaw. The digital media brand originally just focused on YouTube and on London, because they couldn’t afford to go very far, with Burgess in front of camera and Warr largely behind the scenes. Growth was slow and incremental. It took four years before they hit 10,000 subscribers. But when they began posting travel videos, things accelerated quickly. One in particular, 48 Hours in Paris , went viral. It’s since logged 2.6 million views. Unfortunately, this mitzvah was the eve of lockdown. Restaurant content wasn’t a viable plan in 2020, and the guys thought of hanging it up. But when restrictions loosened, a shift back to the U.K. and, pivotally, a focus on Instagram grew the business so that it could be Burgess’ full-time pursuit by 2023. Today, they have almost 1.9 million followers across platforms. They produce travel videos in cities around the world now, but, in world culinary capital of London, TopJaw has arguably become the most valuable resource for recommendations. He’s not just interviewing chefs anymore, either. Every few clips there’s another luminary: Matt Damon, Florence Pugh (twice), Kate Winslet, Theo James. The singer Jessie Ware, who hosts food podcast Table Manners with her mother Lennie, recently mocked Burgess’ rising profile by referring to him as “Mr Michelin” in her visit to TopJaw. (The calls for talent participation, by the way, are almost exclusively incoming.) Knife Edge has already been renewed for a third season , and Burgess will be there to chronicle the professionals he admires succeed and fail — and to eat their food. But when I ask him the obvious question, if this is another paver in the path from content creator to traditional TV host, the suggestion seems to leave him a little indifferent. “There’s so much that I want to do in that world, and I don’t think I’m necessarily attracted to doing more TV,” he says. “There’s a lot of green grass on both sides. Plus, making videos on the internet is awesome.” So is getting to travel and eat for a living. Jesse Burgess in Apple TV’s Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars . Apple TV THR

title: Comcast Co-Founder Julian Brodsky Dies at 93
full_text: × Nov 6, 2026 8:09am PT Comcast Co-Founder Julian Brodsky Dies at 93 By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Comcast Co-Founder Julian Brodsky Dies at 93 9 minutes ago Fox Closes $22 Billion Roku Takeover, Says Streaming Platform Will Remain ‘Open Ecosystem’ 2 hours ago Lionsgate Quarterly Revenue Pops 41% on Strength of ‘Michael,’ TV Series Sales as Studio Narrows Net Loss 18 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Comcast Julian Brodsky , a cable TV pioneer and financial guru who was a co-founding partner of Comcast more than 60 years ago, has died. He was 93. Comcast announced his death Friday. According to the cable and media company, Brodsky died peacefully surrounded by his family while in hospice care on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. Brodsky teamed with Comcast founder Ralph J. Roberts and co-founding partner Daniel Aaron to build the company from its earliest days, beginning with the acquisition of a small cable television system in Tupelo, Mississippi, in 1963. Working from a “modest office” near Philadelphia, the three laid the foundation for what would grow into one of the world’s leading media and technology companies, according to Comcast. Related Stories Pamela Abdy Delivers Fiery Speech After Warner Bros. Exit: ‘It Is Getting Harder, Not Easier, to Be a Woman in the Business’ “Julian was an extraordinary leader, a brilliant financial mind and one of the architects of cable television,” Brian L. Roberts, chairman of Comcast, said in a statement. “He was a trusted partner and close friend to my father, Ralph, and someone I was fortunate to learn from and work alongside for so many years. He was one of the most creative financiers of his generation, but just as important, he established a culture of financial integrity, uncompromising standards, and respect for colleagues that remains at the heart of our company today.” Roberts added, “Julian was a mentor and a friend, and his contributions to our company and our community cannot be overstated. We will miss him deeply, and our thoughts are with his family and everyone who knew and loved him.” Brodsky was born in Philadelphia on July 16, 1933. He attended Overbrook High School and graduated from the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. He served two years in the U.S. Army before beginning his career as a certified public accountant. While working as an auditor, he developed an early fascination with the emerging cable television industry, an interest that would shape the course of his career and help define his legacy. As Comcast’s longtime CFO, Brodsky was instrumental in financing the company’s expansion and efforts to raise capital. The company credits him with helping guide major acquisitions that transformed Comcast from a small regional cable operator into an industry leader. Brodsky was among the industry’s “earliest financial innovators,” according to Comcast, helping establish cable television’s credibility as an investment and demonstrating its long-term potential to banks, institutional investors and Wall Street at a time when the business was still in its infancy. Brodsky played a central role in Comcast’s initial public offering in 1972 and helped establish the company’s reputation for financial integrity and disciplined management, the company said. Along with Ralph Roberts, he formed Comcast Interactive Capital in 1999, now called Comcast Ventures, to invest in early-stage technology companies and obtain a window into opportunities that could potentially benefit Comcast’s business. In 2004, Brodsky became Comcast’s non-executive vice chairman and retired from the company and its board of directors in 2011. Brodksy’s contributions to the cable television industry were recognized with numerous honors, including his induction into the Cable Television Hall of Fame in 2003 and the National Cable & Telecommunications Association’s Distinguished Vanguard Award. Beyond Comcast, Brodsky was a dedicated philanthropist and a champion of the Philadelphia community. Together with his beloved wife of 70 years, Lois, he supported numerous cultural and educational institutions, including the Philadelphia Museum of Art, where he served for nearly three decades as a trustee. In October 2026, the couple announced a $20 million gift to establish the Lois G. and Julian A. Brodsky Learning and Engagement Center, reflecting their longstanding commitment to making art and education accessible to future generations. In addition to Lois, Brodsky is survived by their three daughters, Debra Brodsky, Ellen Brodsky (married to Ted Rybeck) and Laura Brodsky (Michael Beard), and his brother, Marc Brodsky (Vivian Brodsky). He was predeceased by his parents, David and Esther Brodsky. He is also survived by four grandchildren. A private memorial service will be held, and a celebration of Brodsky’s life will be announced at a later date. ‘One Minute to Midnight’ Review: A Stellar Cast Deliver Interesting but Overly Preachy Disquisitions on the Changing Nature of Male-Female Relations Loading comments...

title: Melania Trump Dismisses Media as “Noise” in Trailer for ‘Melania’ Doc Follow-Up
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All November 6, 2026 8:06am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Melania Trump in her eponymous documentary. Prime Video Melania Trump isn’t especially impressed by her media coverage in the trailer for Melania, the two-part docuseries from Prime Video about the first lady that dropped on Friday ahead of a Nov. 20 premiere. “The media, they want gossip. title: Romanian First-Ever Country of Focus at AFM, ‘Fjord’ Director Cristian Mungiu to Attend
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All November 6, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Fjord, Sebastian Stan, 2026. Neon/Courtesy Everett Collection In a surprise move, the American Film Market , traditional home to mainstream cinema in all its schlocky glory, is going upscale arthouse. At next week’s AFM — Nov. 10-15 at the Fairmont Century Plaza in Los Angeles — there will be a focus on Romanian cinema. AFM has named Romania its first-ever country of focus. National film industry group Creative Romanian Filmmakers (CRFM) will bring over a delegation of filmmakers, producers and production companies to present their latest movies and to meet with industry execs to discuss shooting in Romanian and international co-production opportunities. Related Stories Movies 'an open field' Is a Deeply Personal Story of Loss, Grief and Compassion (Exclusive Netflix Trailer) Movies 'Elsinore' to Close Camerimage Festival “Romania has been part of the AFM community for many years, and we’re proud to recognize its contributions to global cinema as our first-ever Country of Focus,” said Jackie Brenneman, President & CEO of the Independent Film & Television Alliance (IFTA), which produces the AFM. “Together with Creative Romanian Filmmakers, we look forward to showcasing the country’s exceptional talent and opportunities for international collaboration.” “Since 2016, Creative Romanian Filmmakers has brought Romanian producers to the world’s most important film markets and festivals, and the American Film Market has always been a key stop on that journey,” added CRFM managing director Mihai Lupu. “Being named Country of Focus this year is a milestone for our entire industry – an invitation to buyers, sales agents and producers to discover Romanian stories, talent and locations, and to build lasting partnerships with us.” The delegation will include Cristian Mungiu , attending with his Palme d’Or winning drama Fjord , starring Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve . Fjord is Romania’s official entry for the Oscar in the best international feature category and is seen as a shoo-in for the Academy long-list, being announced Dec. 15. “This year, a Romanian film was awarded at every major festival,” noted Mungiu. “I believe Romanian films have real potential in international markets – not only at festivals, but with a wider audience. In this sense, Fjord ’s awards-season campaign and its North American theatrical release look promising.” Mungiu also put in a pitch for his country as a shooting location, noting that “not only is the Romanian cash rebate working again, we have also started a conversation with the Romanian authorities about providing upfront cash-flow financing for the rebate, and we hope to see concrete results as early as 2027.” At AFM, Mungiu will take part in a panel, “Beyond the New Wave: Romania as Your Next Production Partner,” on Saturday, Nov. 14, from 4:00–5:00 PM on the Constellation Stage at the Fairmont Century Plaza. Mungiu will be joined by Valentin Savu, General Manager, Romanian Office for Film and Investments in Culture, Alma Bacula, Head of Production & Partner, Icon Films, and leading producers Iuliana Tarnovetchi, Gabriel Popescu and Ionuț Ionescu to discuss opportunities for filming in Romania, and partnering with local producers to accessing the country’s filming incentives. AFM will showcase four Romanian films with screenings at the AMC Century City 15: Comatogen by Igor Cobileanski, Gone Guy by Andrei Dascalescu, Grounded by Ligia Ciornei and The Circle by Valeriu Andriuta. Romanian companies participating in the event at AFM include Augmented Films, Bullsrecords, Idea Film, Nomad Films Global, Profesional Film Partners, Quantum Media Creative, Frame Film, Mavish Ask, Negrea Visuals, Sýmbolon and Tarnovski Marketing Consultancy. At the Fairmont Century Plaza, Romanian companies will have dedicated exhibition space in suites 1005 and 1037 for meetings. THR

title: How John Summit Is Turning Arenas Into the “World’s Biggest Nightclub” for CTRL ESCAPE Tour
full_text: × Skip to main content John Summit during his CTRL ESCAPE Arena Tour. Gautthiierr “I’m always about doing things first and really breaking the mold and breaking barriers, especially in the DJ world,” John Summit says. That mentality spawned the 32-year-old DJ’s idea to embark on his first-ever arena tour. For any DJ, organizing a global arena tour is a tall order, as their home away from home is typically nightclubs and music festivals. While Summit has become a fixture in those spaces in recent years, he also saw an opportunity for something bigger. Following one-off shows at New York’s Madison Square Garden and Los Angeles’ Kia Forum, Summit admits he didn’t even want to flirt with the idea of a full arena run initially because there are a limited number of DJs capable of pulling off a tour on a similar scale to massive mainstream pop acts. Related Stories Music Singer Jackson Wang Signs With WME (Exclusive) Music With 'The Girl of Your Dreams,' Ashe Finds Her Sweet Spot: "I'm A Really Solid Version of Myself" Sure, a handful of DJs such as The Chainsmokers and Kaskade have launched their own versions of arena and stadium tours. Still, Summit considers his multi-country CTRL ESCAPE Arena Tour a particularly unique and ambitious opportunity, as he’s the sole headliner on each date, and it’s strictly a DJ set rather than mixed in with pop performances. John Summit during his CTRL ESCAPE Arena Tour. Julian Bajsel “There’s been DJs who’ve played arenas, but to this scale and this level, this is a very ambitious tour and it’s not something I technically have to do because obviously the clubs and festivals and everything has been working so well,” Summit tells The Hollywood Reporter . “But because I did those one-off shows and they worked out super well, I knew that I had the confidence to actually take the show on the road.” Luckily for Summit, the tour’s visual concept came easily as his sophomore album CTRL ESCAPE already had a theme centered around breaking out of the corporate 9-to-5 “matrix.” The notion was personal for Summit, as he left his job as a CPA in 2019 to follow his passion for music — and it clearly worked out. “The fans can relate as well too because you’re going to that show; they probably all worked their 9-to-5 during the day to then be able to afford the ticket at night,” Summit says. “So it’s going to be that show is their way of breaking out of that.” It was important for Summit to build a world that his fans could truly escape into, so he leaned on his creative director, Alex Alvga, who also worked on his sophomore album and other shows, to channel the corporate-to-rave transformation that originated in his “LIGHTS GO OUT” music video. John Summit during his CTRL ESCAPE Arena Tour. Jamal Eid “We used the music video to drive the whole rollout of the album, and from there we just built the whole narrative,” Alvga tells THR . “Then for the arenas, we just wanted to keep building on that.” The attention was in the detail, from Summit’s mixing table looking like an old computer monitor to the speakers having a ’90s computer casing around them, to backup dancers wearing corporate attire dancing in cubicle-like structures. “We have a lot of stuff that plays into that same aesthetic that we’ve been playing up until now, because of course the best thing as a fan is just when everything feels cohesive,” Alvga says. But the team didn’t slack on lighting, automation, lasers, pyro and practical effects either, a necessity for what is essentially a massive dance party. Summit delivers several immersive moments throughout the show, from dropping 1,200 employee performance review papers over the crowd to a fired/hired bit with audience members who aren’t dancing enough. All these elements are key components for the narrative Summit aims to tell during his four-act performance. “I can’t really think of any DJs who really do an actual story throughout a set,” the DJ says. Alvga says it “starts with a control, then we go into the escape section and then we go into the Experts Only section,” which is act three and will feature Summit in the crowd at the much more intimate B stage. “By that moment in the show, the narrative already explains the workers have escaped. Now it’s time to party and have fun,” the creative director says of the fourth and final act, titled “release.” With the visuals, design and story set, the last — and arguably the most important — piece of the puzzle is the music. John Summit during his CTRL ESCAPE Arena Tour. Julian Bajsel When it comes to his other shows, Summit often finalizes the set hours before taking the stage and “it’s not even an official set list because I get on stage and I switch it up,” he says. However, with a tour of this scale, there’s much more at play behind the scenes. “Honestly, the biggest challenge for me is getting the music done ahead of time and then not going full improv with it,” Summit says. Thankfully for his team, this DJ found his perfect mix. “I know how I’m going to start, I know I’m going to finish [and] I know the big moments in the middle,” he says, while also weaving in moments “to get a little spicy with it and creative.” As Summit sets out on this new chapter, he’s excited to learn and grow with each show. As for his fans, he hopes that by the end of the night, “the phones are down, you’re dancing, you’re in the moment.” John Summit during his CTRL ESCAPE Arena Tour. Gautthiierr Fans will also need to be locked in so they don’t miss potential surprises, special guests and an outfit change or two. “I’m starting in my [accountant] suit and I guarantee you I won’t be finishing it in the suit,” Summit quips. However, despite having a group of backup dancers, don’t expect Summit to debut a whole dance routine. “I’ll do my typical fist bump, don’t worry,” he says with a laugh. “But no breakdancing or anything. I’m not going to go full Tate McRae or anything.” That’s the fans’ responsibility — lest they get fired by the boss on the first day now. He says, “It’s kind of cool to turn an arena into the world’s biggest nightclub for a night.” THR

The pair will work together to develop short-form content, often from emerging horror filmmaking talent, and seek to expand that into feature films. As part of the agreement, TerrorBox will release Vasaria’s short film Jezebel as a vertical series on the platform. Vasaria will explore select TerrorBox titles for potential feature film development. Box Entertainment Group , which Ryan Justice set up in 2025 launched TerrorBox earlier this year as a microdrama service dedicated to horror. Rist. The streamer has also bought the Nightmarish TV library of vertical horror shorts. Created by Atlanta-based filmmakers Madison Hoover and Jaime Lucero Jr., this comprises bite-sized horror stories designed specifically for vertical viewing, typically running 90 seconds or less. She claimed that in 2018, a letter about her father was sent to the Metropolitan Police and its Royalty and Specialist Protection unit and was “subsequently shared” with her. “It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” Meghan said. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.” The Metropolitan Police said at the time that they were “undertaking enquiries internally in an effort to confirm” that a letter had been passed from their officers to Meghan. It is understood that the Met has not and is not currently investigating Thomas Markle Sr. Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018, when he failed to walk her down the aisle at her wedding. She was escorted by King Charles instead. Thomas Markle has never met her and Prince Harry ’s two children. Last year, she sent a letter to him while he was in the hospital getting his left lower leg amputated due to a blood clot. “Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children,” Meghan concluded. The FBI also issued a statement last month saying that they were “aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of U.S. law.” Representatives for Meghan Markle and the FBI did not immediately respond to Variety ’s request for comment on Markle Sr.’s arrest. title: Carson Daly, Laura Jarrett Ready to Launch ‘New Era’ at NBC’s ‘Saturday Today’
full_text: × Nov 6, 2026 7:40am PT Carson Daly, Laura Jarrett Ready to Launch ‘New Era’ at NBC’s ‘Saturday Today’ By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Carson Daly, Laura Jarrett Ready to Launch ‘New Era’ at NBC’s ‘Saturday Today’ 35 minutes ago Jim Cramer Leads CNBC Into Creator-Media Era 2 hours ago Did Midterm Elections Cause Changes in News World Order? 18 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of NBC News Carson Daly was looking for a new challenge in a long career in the media business. On Saturday morning, he’ll get it. Daly will team up with Laura Jarrett , Joe Fryer, and meteorologist Angie Lassman on NBC’s “Saturday Today” telecast, the latest attempt by one of the big broadcast networks to create bespoke versions of their morning franchises that appeal to weekend audiences with a little more time on their hands in the A.M. “If people are waking up with us, we want to respect that and we want to give them something that’s worth tuning into,” says Jarrett, who joined “Today” in 2023, a year after moving to NBC News from CNN. Related Stories Pamela Abdy Delivers Fiery Speech After Warner Bros. Exit: ‘It Is Getting Harder, Not Easier, to Be a Woman in the Business’ NBC, ABC and CBS have worked to create weekend-news programs with a little more distinction from their weekday flagships. The Saturday telecast of CBS’ “Saturday Morning” puts a spotlight on topics such as food and music. ABC recently recalibrated the anchor teams on its weekend broadcasts of “Good Morning America,” adding Rachel Scott and Rhiannon Ally. NBC has been encouraged in this vision by the Sunday telecast of “Today,” led by Willie Geist . The anchor offers a slower-paced hour of “Today” that tackles headlines as warranted, but also offers up a deeper interview with a person of interest as well as other features. Geist typically writes much of the show by himself. NBC News has experimented with turning Geist’s longer-form interviews into ticketed events , a move that generates live-media revenue. Adding Daly, however, brings a person with a different set of skills to the fore of the Saturday show. Jarrett’s previous co-host, Peter Alexander, had a long tenure as a Washington and White House correspondent . Daly has cultivated a broader set of experiences, famously hosting MTV’s “TRL” earlier in his career, then going to host the wee-hours NBC program “Last Call” and host and executive produce “The Voice.” Over that time, he’s learned to lead in-depth conversations and hold forth with musicians, newsmakers and entertainers. “I’ve always enjoyed longer-form interviews,” Daly says, and he studied Bob Costas and Greg Kinnear, who hosted late-night shows at NBC before his tenure started. “I have a natural curiosity,’” he says, and often comes into a segment with “one thousand questions” he might want to ask a guest — if only “Today” had more time for extended interviews Daly has been a staple on “Today” since 2013, when he joined as a correspondent of sorts, curating interesting developments taking place on social media from the show’s “Orange Room.” These days, he’s more of a regular presence in the weekday telecast’s second hour, and is often found talking alongside Savannah Guthrie, Craig Melvin, Al Roker and other “Today” anchors. Several months ago, he considered how he might push himself, and asked “Today” producers if they would consider letting him co-anchor on days when others were off — even on holidays. “I’ve never been afraid to take on a challenge,” Daly says. “I’m glad I stuck my neck out.” Jarrett has been enjoying her time on “Today” as well as her position as NBC News’ senior legal correspondent. Saturday viewers can still expect to get the headlines, she says. “We will still do the news. We will still do special reports” if warranted, she says. Jarrett has “a style on TV that I happen to not only respect but also enjoy watching, and so I think I’m going to learn a lot,” says Daly. Daly takes up his new duties just as the holiday season approaches, a cycle that often brings a broader audience to “Today.” On Saturday, says Jarrett, viewers might get a peek at the Rockefeller Center Christmas Tree arriving in New York — in addition to the official launch of “a new era” for the Saturday program. ‘One Minute to Midnight’ Review: A Stellar Cast Deliver Interesting but Overly Preachy Disquisitions on the Changing Nature of Male-Female Relations Loading comments...

title: ‘Werwulf,’ ‘Cliff Booth,’ ‘The Odyssey’ and More Costume Designers Show Exclusive Sketches From the Year’s Biggest Movies
full_text: × Cliff Booth: Gloria Kim; Odyssey: I Ellen Mirojnick; Sense and Sensibility: Courtesy of Focus Features Ruffled gowns, sequins and a werewolf hunter dressed in layers of wool are among this year’s costume designs audiences will see on screen. Contemporary designs are seen in Olivia Wilde in “The Invite,” while a nod to the Regency era is made in “Sense and Sensibility.” And there are numbers. Marci Rodgers delivered over 3,000 looks for the “Michael” biopic starring Jaafar Jackson, while Ellen Mirojnick created over 5,300 designs for Christopher Nolan’s epic, “The Odyssey.” Related Stories Pamela Abdy Delivers Fiery Speech After Warner Bros. Exit: ‘It Is Getting Harder, Not Easier, to Be a Woman in the Business’ Below, Mirojnick, Rodgers and more costume designers share exclusive looks at their concepts for costumes which reflect character arcs and show how clothing can tell a lot about a person before they have even spoken a single line. The Odyssey Gowns were crafted to reflect Anne Hathaway’s sweeping character arc Costume designer Ellen Mirojnick says that though Anne Hathaway’s Penelope had inner strength at the start of Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” “it was important that she never appear queen-like.” As the film opens, Penelope’s “dresses were more vulnerable, simpler, not at all decorative. Her work at the loom was softer — it was artistic in a way.” By the time she sets forth to challenge her suitors, though, her gown is a “magnificent blue.” “That was quite intentional,” Mirojnick says. “It was to be the period at the end of the sentence. She needed to look armor-like.” Michael Re-creating the King of Pop’s Motown moment One key scene in Antoine Fuqua’s biopic about Michael Jackson was his performance of “Billie Jean” at the “Motown 25” concert in 1983. There, Jackson debuted not only his moonwalk but his signature outfit: a black sequined jacket, a fedora, a single glove, white socks, cropped pants and black loafers. Costume designer Marci Rodgers says she approached recreating the look “from the feet up.” She used the same shoe Jackson wore: a Florsheim Como Imperial loafer. The pants “were a version of the tuxedo pants that we see when he’s singing ‘Off the Wall’ — it’s the same style.” It turns out that the jacket Jackson wore during the performance belonged to his mother, Katherine. “To me, it was like his cape,” Rodgers says. “He was wearing a piece of clothing that was from his mother’s closet, and that, by far, transformed everything.” Jaafar Jackson, who plays Michael, had a similar jacket and lent it to Rodgers to study. “It was in my possession, so I was able to get as close as possible to re-creating the sequins of Michael’s mother’s jacket.” Wicker A fierce woman with a woven husband In “Wicker,” a spinster fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) in a medieval community, mocked by villagers for her independence, asks the local basket weaver (Peter Dinklage) to make her a husband (Alexander Skarsgård) out of wicker. Writer-directors Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson wanted the fisherwoman’s husband to be created practically, rather than with special effects. So prosthetic makeup designer Joe Dunckley and lead makeup FX artist Sarah Rubano spent 18 months developing Skarsgård’s costume. It started with a full-body scan of the actor’s frame so they could sculpt pieces specific to him. The intricate weave was created using a relatively new powder-bed printing process. Dunckley explains, “It’s a volume of thermoplastic elastomer. You shoot a laser into it, and where that focal point of the laser is, it fuses the powder and you can build intricate weave and complex geometry.” In the end, 95% of the costume was made using 50 3D-printed appliances painted to look like wicker and stitched to a spandex suit. The key, Dunckley says, was not to lose Skarsgård under the makeup. Sense and Sensibility Updating Jane Austen At the start of Georgia Oakley’s adaptation of Jane Austen’s classic novel, the Dashwood women (Daisy Edgar-Jones, Esmé Creed-Miles and Caitríona Balfe) are mourning the loss of their father and husband, which meant that there were rules that costume designer Grace Snell had to follow: no shiny buttons, the fabric had to be dull and black was one of the few acceptable colors, along with gray and lavender. “I wanted Mrs. Dashwood to be the deepest shade of grief,” Snell says. So the designer fashioned a black taffeta dress. “What’s great about this black is it’s almost got this stripe of dark green in it, so it looks quite reflective. It felt like it could have been from any time.” Mrs. Dashwood stays in mourning for most of the film, but as the story progresses, Snell began introducing beige into her palette. Willoughby (Frank Dillane), who toys with young Marianne, “has a real interest in fashion,” Snell says “and wants to be seen.” For the London hop scene between Willoughby and Marianne, Snell put the young man in a rust-red moleskin coat. Opposite Marianne’s pink dress, “they look wonderful, but it looks explosive.” She completed Willoughby’s outfit with silk pantaloons. “They were only just coming into fashion, so he’s one of the first to bring them over from France,” Snell says, adding, “He’s a little bit of a rock star; he’s unattainable.” Werwulf A wealthy man is chosen to hunt the beast killing poor townsfolk This companion piece to Robert Eggers’ 2024 “Nosferatu” tells the tale of a 14th-century town beset by a werewolf. Willem Dafoe plays the landowner-hunter hired by the king to lead the charge against the beast. What sets Dafoe’s character apart from the film’s victims is the amount of wool he wears. “His is the character that really denotes wealth,” says costume designer Linda Muir. Because wool was a scarce commodity at the time, Muir put him in double-layered wool coats and linen shirts. His boots, too, are higher than those of anyone else in the film to emphasize his station. The props department made him a family signet ring, and to complete the look, Muir gave him a bycocket, which is commonly associated with Robin Hood. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth Booth’s beer-bottle shirt is his version of the Dude’s robe David Fincher’s follow-up to “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” starring Brad Pitt, is no longer about a cocky stunt double, Cliff Booth — now the stunt man is tending bar. Fincher’s instructions to costume designer Trish Summerville were to keep things authentic and grounded. “Cliff’s character is very lived in,” Summerville says. So she retained elements of Cliff’s character from the first film, like his love for Hawaiian shirts. “Back then, people didn’t have disposable fashion; you kept your clothes for quite a while. Cliff still has his favorite jeans — Levi’s — moccasins and work shirts.” In one scene, Cliff wears a Hawaiian shirt featuring beer bottles. Searching for the perfect shirt, Summerville found various rayon numbers from the ’50s through the ’70s printed with images of bottles of booze. But she needed multiples of the garment for Pitt and his own stunt double. “So I had an artist put them all together, and we printed the graphics on [new] shirts.” She adds, “It made me laugh. Cliff’s a chill rascal, so I thought the shirt was just great for him.” The Invite In Olivia Wilde’s latest, costumes and interiors work together as camouflage Atsushi Nishijima When Angela (Olivia Wilde) and her husband, Joe (Seth Rogen) — a couple on edge — invite their loud upstairs neighbors (Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton) to an intimate dinner party, things take an unexpected turn. In early meetings with Wilde, costume designer Arianne Phillips came to understand how the doorways and windows of Angela’s apartment created “beautiful framing” — so much so that Phillips thought of the costumes like portraits or photographs. “Olivia really loved the idea that Angela’s creative identity is so absorbed into the apartment that she basically blends into the walls,” Phillips says. “There’s a funny scene with her and Joe in the bedroom when she’s asking him about the paint color, and all the colors are so close, you can’t tell them apart. That was reflected in her blouse too.” Loading comments...

title: ‘an open field’ Is a Deeply Personal Story of Loss, Grief and Compassion (Exclusive Netflix Trailer)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All November 6, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'an open field' Courtesy of Netflix In March 2019, a Boeing 737 MAX crashed in Ethiopia just six minutes after taking off from the airport in the country’s capital, Addis Ababa. It had 157 people on board, and all of them died. Among them was Max Thabiso Edkins . His older brother Teboho Edkins decided to make a film about the experience of grief and mourning that his family and the local community went through. The result is the very personal 38-minute short film an open field , directed by Edkins and produced by his father, Don Edkins, and Carine Chichkowsky. The film is now going global, hitting Netflix on Dec. 1, about a year after its world premiere at the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam ( IDFA ) 2025, where it won the best short documentary award. Related Stories Business Netflix Taps Mattel's Roberto Stanichi to Lead Consumer Products and Experiences Business Dark Slope to Open New Virtual Production Stage in Vancouver (Exclusive) The title of the movie becomes clear when you watch it. In an open field, the filmmaker finds out that dozens of nearby villagers immediately converged on the crash site to help. Some even stood vigil for a month to protect and preserve the area. Years later, they continue to mourn alongside family members who visit the site, including Edkins and his father, also making the film a story about collective grief and compassion. “Boeing’s widely criticized response to the crash stands in sharp contrast to the community’s enduring compassion,” highlights a synopsis. “Both a personal essay on loss and an exploration of the potential healing power of collective mourning, Edkins’s film is a quiet testament to humanity – moments of warmth, resolve, grief, fear, patience, and simple acts of kindness.” Indeed, the film feels like a cinematic attempt to connect with a late brother and son’s spirit. In that sense, an open field is a family film. And it may be set in a far-away place for many viewers, but it transcends borders, given that the plane’s passengers came from more than 30 countries and that anyone who has lost a loved one has faced the burden of that loss. ‘an open field’ Courtesy of Netflix an open field is a South Africa-France-Germany production by Day Zero Film and Video Productions in South Africa, Day Zero Films UG in Germany and Survivance in France. The cinematographer is Jide Akinleminu, the editor is Anne Fabini. The film, shot in color and black-and-white, features dialogue in both English and Amharic. “This is a delicate and personal work and about something fundamental to being human,” says director Teboho Edkins. “I hope that the film can find its way to as many people as possible, and that something in it might resonate with them. Having Netflix bring the film to its global audiences is very meaningful to me, and I’m grateful for their support as it makes its way out into the world.” THR can now exclusively premiere a trailer for an open field ahead of its Netflix debut. title: ‘Dune’ Star Chang Chen Introduces Six Rising Taiwanese Actors In Golden Horse & TCCF Showcase
full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz Weta FX CEO Daniel Seah Unpacks TAICCA Partnership: “Taiwan Has Creative Talent, Technology & Government Support” Taiwan Creative Content Fest Opens With Focus On IP, Co-Production & Pledges Of Government Support Weta FX Partners With TAICCA To Position Taiwan As AI Hub; Expands Partnership With Moonshine Studio View All November 6, 2026 6:53am Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: Rosen, Ho Man-Xi, Lin Yi-Ting, Chang Chen, Sue Wang, Bai Xiao-ying, Ma Shih-yuan, Jimmy Liu Deadline Taiwanese star Chang Chen introduced six rising actors in a showcase co-organized by the Golden Horse Awards and Taiwan Creative Content Fest ( TCCF ) at the seventh edition of TCCF today. The event, which marks the first collaboration between TCCF and Taiwan’s Golden Horse Awards, aims to raise the profile of Taiwanese actors at a time when they’re becoming a key factor in structuring international co-productions. The six talents included actresses Bai Xiao-ying ( Girl ), Ho Man-xi ( Sunshine Women’s Choir ), Ma Shih-yuan ( Left-Handed Girl ), and Lin Yi-ting ( A Dance With Rainbows ), along with actors Rosen ( Marching Boys ) and Jimmy Liu ( Blind Love ). Related Stories News Weta FX CEO Daniel Seah Unpacks TAICCA Partnership: "Taiwan Has Creative Talent, Technology & Government Support" News Taiwan Creative Content Fest Opens With Focus On IP, Co-Production & Pledges Of Government Support Bai and Ho are both nominated for Best New Performer at this year’s Golden Horse Awards, while the remaining four talents were all nominated last year, with Ma winning in the category. Watch on Deadline “We’re seeing more co-productions involving Taiwan and it’s encouraging to see this kind of exchange,” said Chang, whose recent credits include Dune and Cannes Directors Fortnight title Lucky Lu . “It’s important for us to learn more about each other, particularly in international co-productions, to avoid misunderstandings that could delay the production process.” Sue Wang, Chair of TCCF organizer the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA), said: “Taiwanese actors are one of the elements that could be used to apply for TAICCA funding, so we need to raise the profile of our acting talent and create more opportunities for them to be seen.” During the showcase, each of the actors talked about their acting, language and other professional skills and the kind of projects they hope to work on in the future. Bai speaks fluent Japanese, while Rosen and Ma both speak English. Liu was winning Taekwondo competitions before landing a role in Disney+ series American Born Chinese alongside Michelle Yeoh. Chang, who is currently serving as Chair of the Taipei Golden Horse Film Festival Executive Committee, gave the six young actors a few career tips. “It’s not about whether a project is international or not, it’s about being adaptive to different production teams.” He also passed on some advice that he was given by a director early in his career: “Read autobiographies of as many people as you can. As an actor, you need to experience different lives throughout your career, but at your young age, your experience of life is limited. title: Fox Corp. Closes $22 Billion Acquisition Of Roku
full_text: Skip to main content By Dade Hayes Dade Hayes Business Editor @dadehayes More Stories By Dade Fox Corp. Closes $22 Billion Acquisition Of Roku Online Media Pioneer Salon To Shutter: “Our Publishing Model Is No Longer Sustainable” Netflix Woos Mattel Veteran Roberto Stanichi To Lead Consumer Products and Experiences View All November 6, 2026 6:42am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images/Deadline Fox Corp. has closed its $22 billion acquisition of Roku , creating a massive new player in streaming. Shares in Roku, which was founded more than two decades ago, will stop trading on the Nasdaq as of Friday. Related Stories News How Fox’s $22 Billion Deal For Roku Raises The Floor For Its Content, Advertising Revenue & Creator Division Executives Both Sides Of Fox’s $22B Roku Acquisition Call It A Streaming Win-Win, But Wall Street Has Questions Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch earlier this week indicated that regulators outside the U.S. had blessed the merger, and there were reports that the U.S. Department of Justice also was nearing sign-off. But the closing came less than five months after the deal was proposed last June – well ahead of the initially projected window of the first half of 2027. Roku founder and CEO Anthony Wood will be involved with the combined operation, joining Fox’s board of directors and becoming Co-Chair of Fox Digital Platforms. The newly formed division includes properties like Roku, Tubi, Fox One, and Red Seat Ventures. Paul Cheesbrough is now Co-Chair and CEO of the digital division. Watch on Deadline While Wood is staying on, plenty of questions remain about how Fox intends to structure executive teams in advertising, product and many other areas. Tubi, the free, ad-supported service Fox acquired in 2020, has thrived as a San Francisco-based group granted a degree of autonomy by its parent company. One exec who could factor into the combination is Charlie Collier. The former CEO of Fox Entertainment has been president of Roku Media since 2022. Ahead of the deal, Roku said its platform reaches more than 100 million households, most of them in the U.S. but also in several other countries. The official announcement of the deal’s close said it marks the beginning of “a new transformational era” for Fox. The transaction creates “an innovative, scaled media and technology company with superior reach, engagement and monetization capabilities,” the company added. Fox expects to realize merger-related cost savings of $400 million within two years, and also sees the deal helping its free cash flow per share by 2028. “The closing of this acquisition advances the long-term strategy of Fox,” Murdoch said. “Beginning today, our top priority for the combined company is to continue to relentlessly serve audiences and partners, while reinforcing the openness and choice that is the essence of the Roku platform. Our shared entrepreneurial passion and clear conviction toward building the future together with our new Roku colleagues gives us great confidence in the opportunities ahead of us.” Under terms of the merger agreement, Roku stockholders are entitled to receive $95.30 in cash and 0.9799 shares of Fox Class A common stock for each share of Roku Class A and Roku Class B common stock they owned immediately prior to closing. As a result of the transaction, Fox stockholders own about 74% of the outstanding shares of Fox common stock and former Roku stockholders own about 26%. Wood added in a statement, “We started Roku more than two decades ago to give people a better way to watch TV, and that mission doesn’t change today. What does change is our reach and resources. Fox has a deep respect for Roku’s culture and wholly shares our commitment to staying open to every content partner. Our teams will keep building and innovating as they always have, now with the support and capabilities of Fox behind us. title: Katherine Ryan Feeling “Grief & Relief” Over Russell Brand Conviction After Calling Him A “Sexual Predator” On Comedy Central’s ‘Roast Battle’
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Katherine Ryan Feeling “Grief & Relief” Over Russell Brand Conviction After Calling Him A “Sexual Predator” On Comedy Central’s ‘Roast Battle’ Bear Grylls Speaks Out After Getting Heat For Baptizing Russell Brand: “It Is Right That Justice Has Been Served” Russell Brand Trial: Katy Perry Omitted By Prosecutors View All November 6, 2026 6:36am Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: Russell Brand with Katherine Ryan and Jimmy Carr on 'Roast Battle' Comedy Central Katherine Ryan has said she is feeling “grief and relief” after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault in London on Thursday. Watch on Deadline “It really made me feel just quite dysregulated again, caught off-guard, emotional, in awe of the survivors who also had nothing to gain,” she said. “They came forward despite Russell Brand having fame, power, money, and a legion of fans ready to attack them.” Ryan continued: “I will never be someone who like, dances on graves. There has been some justice done today. There’s a level of relief, but there’s grief alongside relief. Everything’s nuanced, and it was proved in court that a terrible thing happened, and that means that a terrible thing happened. “I just think again and again about people who have been hurt, and who have to carry that, who’ve carried that around long enough, and will continue to carry that in some way, regardless of what justice is done.” Deadline reported how Brand was dropped from Roast Battle after Ryan torched him on camera over allegations that he had sexually assaulted women. Her jokes did not make the final edit. One person familiar with the matter said Brand was “absolutely furious” at being targeted by Ryan. Ryan had previously spoken about her experience on Roast Battle , but did not name Brand or the show she was working on. In an appearance on BBC series Louis Theroux Interviews.. ., Ryan revealed that she confronted her unnamed co-star: “I – in front of loads of people, in the format of the show – said to this person’s face that they are a predator.” She revisited the subject during her Sky stand-up special last year . Ryan explained: “I was invited on a panel show, and I was so excited to do it, but then I found out that if I went on, I would be sat next to a man whom I firmly believe, but can’t prove to be a c***. And that’s the lawyer’s choice of words, not mine.” She continued: “Initially, I turned the job down, and then I thought: well, he’ll be there in his unnecessarily tight jeans, won’t he? Ryan said Brand was “fine with it for a while, until eventually he had a hissy fit and threatened to quit the show.” She continued: “The channel got upset. They didn’t want him to leave, and they issued him a new contract, which he waltzed into my dressing room and threw under my nose the next day. He said: ‘Look, you’re not allowed to be mean to me anymore, because I don’t consent.’” Ryan added that she had to “be nice” following Comedy Central’s intervention on the show, produced by Fulwell Entertainment. title: ‘Buena Vista Social Club’ to Close on Broadway in January
full_text: × Skip to main content By Caitlin Huston Plus Icon Caitlin Huston Business Writer hustonca Follow Sign Up View All November 6, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The Broadway company of 'Buena Vista Social Club.' Matthew Murphy Buena Vista Social Club will play its final performance Jan. 17 after close to two years on Broadway . The musical, inspired by the titular Cuban band, took home five Tony Awards in 2025, including a special Tony for its onstage band. While the show is closing in January, producers say it is on track to recoup before closure, making it the second musical of the 2024-2025 to announce recoupment. The show also has a touring production, and currently has productions in Puerto Rico and Mexico City. In 2027, the musical will open in London’s West End. Buena Vista Social Club is the first show on Broadway to feature a score sung entirely in Spanish. The story is based on the creation of the Buena Vista Social Club’s 1997 album, which was made up of legends in the 1950s Cuban music scene and toggles between the creation of the album and the past. The musical opened on March 19, 2025, at the Gerald Schoenfeld Theatre, after starting previews in February 2025. The musical is still commanding high attendance, though its grosses have gradually fallen from the highs of 2025. It is the second musical of its season to recoup, following Just In Time , which is still running. The show features a book by Marco Ramirez, direction by Saheem Ali and choreography by Patricia Delgado and Justin Peck. Lead producer Orin Wolf also hinted at a possible film deal. “From our very first trip to Cuba to meet the musicians who created this masterpiece, I knew we had something truly special, something to cherish. I am in awe of what Marco R., Saheem, Patricia, Justin, David, Marco P. and Dean have created artistically, bringing this extraordinary music to life on stage and presenting the first Broadway score performed exclusively in Spanish,” said Wolf. “I am deeply grateful for the time we’ve had on Broadway – and the speed with which the team has created three more productions. We are thrilled the Broadway production is on schedule to recoup as we look ahead to an exciting tour, special engagements in Mexico and Puerto Rico, the film and so much more.” In addition to the onstage band, the cast of Buena Vista Social Club currently includes Gina Torres (Omara), Rick Negron (Compay), Mel Semé (Ibrahim), Jainardo Batista Sterling (Rubén), Isa Antonetti (Young Omara), Da’Von T. Moody (Young Compay), Wesley Wray (Young Ibrahim), Jesús Pupo (Young Rubén), Renesito Avich (Eliades), Tanairi Sade Vazquez (Young Haydee), Chris Myers (Juan de Marcos) and José “Candelita” Iglesias (The Narrator). title: Apple TV Renews ‘Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars’ for Season 3
full_text: Skip to main content By Mikey O'Connell Plus Icon Mikey O'Connell Senior Entertainment Editor View All November 6, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jesse Burgess in Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars Kristin Silady Logo text As the Michelin Guide continues to expand to new cities, so must its television series. Apple TV has given the official green light to season three of its culinary docuseries, Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars . The series, which comes from executive producer Gordon Ramsay , takes cameras around the globe and into the kitchens of the chefs fighting for the most prestigious accolade in restaurants: a Michelin star. Some chefs are going for their first, some are going for more and many are just trying to hold onto their cred. Hosted by TopJaw frontman and co-founder Jesse Burgess , the first two eight-episode seasons are streaming on Apple TV now. “I’m absolutely delighted that Apple TV audiences and chefs from all around the world have truly embraced Knife Edge,” Ramsay said in a statement. “Taking viewers on the journey towards Michelin stars is like climbing aboard an epic rollercoaster. You’d better hold on tight, because it’s one hell of a ride.” Related Stories TV Toni Collette to Lead Apple TV Dramedy 'Lenni' TV 'Monarch: Legacy of Monsters' Eyes Season 3 Shakeup -- If It's Renewed What distinguishes the show, easily Apple TV’s most ambitious entry into the popular food space, is the access its been given by The Michelin Guide. After all, this is an institution that prizes itself on secrecy, deploying its undercover diners to restaurants the world in hopes of getting an accurate reporting of a typical dining experience. “What I love most about making Knife Edge is that, however much time I spend in restaurants around the world, I’m constantly surprised by the extraordinary people and stories we discover,” said Burgess. “Behind every restaurant is a very personal journey, and for the chefs we follow, a Michelin Star can represent years of sacrifice, obsession and an enormous amount of hard work.” Knife Edge has been a unique entry into the Apple TV catalog, marrying travel, culinary competition and docudrama. It’s been enough to attain a 100 percent critics score on Rotten Tomatoes and earn a nomination at the BAFT Television Awards. The series is produced by Apple TV by Studio Ramsay Global, a Fox Entertainment Company. Executive producers are Ramsay, Lisa Edwards, Lorraine Charker-Phillips and Jill Greenwood, with James Callum serving as the series director. The season two finale dropped on the steamer Friday. THR

title: ‘Stranger Things’ Spinoff Series ‘Other Worlds’ Set in the 1950s Ordered by Netflix
full_text: Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All November 6, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Noah Schnapp as Will Byers and Winona Ryder as Joyce Byers in 'Stranger Things.' Courtesy of Netflix Logo text Stranger Things is returning to Netflix . The streamer has officially ordered a live-action prequel series to its massive sci-fi hit (see announcement video below). Titled Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure , the new series will be set in the 1950s, with production taking place in New Mexico. Original series creators and showrunners The Duffer Brothers will serve as co-creators, but have otherwise handed over creative duties to longtime Stranger Things writer Kate Trefry, who also penned the Stranger Things: The First Shadow stage play, and Golden Globe-winning director Joe Wright ( Atonement ), who will helm the first three episodes. Related Stories Business Netflix Taps Mattel's Roberto Stanichi to Lead Consumer Products and Experiences Movies 'La Bola Negra' Ups Planned Theater Count Heading Into Netflix Film's Widest Weekend Yet (Exclusive) The series will feature an all-new cast and story. Details are being kept under wraps, but the title, 1950s New Mexico setting, and one hint by the Duffers in their statement (“watch the skies”) sure do suggest the show has a UFO/aliens/outer space theme. “We’ve been dreaming of Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure for many years now, and to see it become a reality is surreal and exhilarating,” said Matt and Ross Duffer in a statement. “We’re so grateful to our incredible team of collaborators: our showrunner Kate Trefry, who has been in the trenches with us since season two and wrote Stranger Things: The First Shadow ; and our director, Joe Wright, a brilliant artist whose work we’ve long admired. We can’t wait for you to see what they’re cooking up. It’s Stranger Things , but also thrillingly fresh, with a new setting, new heroes and villains, and new… actually, we’re not allowed to say any more. Now, on to casting. In the meantime — watch the skies, nerds!” Last year, Duffers signed a deal to officially jump from Netflix to Paramount as part of a four-year deal with the studio which covers film, TV and streaming projects. “ Stranger Things has always belonged to the fans, and their passion made it a worldwide phenomenon,” said Netflix scripted head Jinny Howe. “Today, on Stranger Things Day, we’re honored to partner again with Matt and Ross Duffer and Kate Trefry to give fans a new dimension of this universe to step into. Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure takes us to the 1950s with new heroes and all the heart, mystery, and spectacle of the original series.” Added Trefry: “The Duffer Brothers gave me my first paying job in Hollywood, and it has been a joy and a fever dream ever since. Now, it is my insane honor and privilege to be bringing this new chapter of Stranger Things to life alongside them and our incredible director Joe Wright. With the support of Netflix and 21Laps, we have had the time of our lives returning to all the horror, wonder and mystery of the flagship, while also telling a wholly new story, one we hope will blow your minds and break your hearts all over again.” Executive producers include The Duffer Brothers via Upside Down Pictures, Shawn Levy and his 21 Laps company, and Paul Dichter, Shelley Meals, Andrea Sperling and Pavlina Hatoupis. Stranger Things debuted in 2016 and became Netflix’s biggest show, delivering 1.2 billion views globally during its first four seasons. The show aired its series finale earlier this year. THR
